question: According to the manual, which of the following is listed as a surface that provides poor traction?
choice_d: Wet pavement, particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes away
explanation: Surfaces that provide poor traction include wet pavement (particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road), gravel, mud, leaves, snow, ice, and painted lane markings or steel plates when wet.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Why should a rider reduce speed before entering a slippery or wet curve?
choice_a: The motorcycle needs more distance to stop, and reducing speed lessens the chance of skidding
choice_b: It has no real effect on skid risk
choice_c: It is only necessary in snow, never in rain
choice_d: Speed reduction is only relevant for passengers, not solo riders
explanation: Reduce speed before you get to a slippery surface to lessen your chances of skidding -- your motorcycle needs more distance to stop, and it's particularly important to slow before entering wet curves.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: On a slippery surface, why should a rider avoid sudden changes in speed or direction?
choice_a: Sudden changes are only dangerous above 60 mph
choice_b: Any sudden change can cause a skid
choice_c: Sudden changes have no bearing on skid risk on slippery surfaces
choice_d: Sudden changes only matter when carrying cargo
explanation: Avoid sudden moves -- any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid. Be as smooth as possible when speeding up, shifting gears, turning, or braking.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: When it starts to rain, where is it usually best to ride?
choice_a: As far right as possible, regardless of debris
choice_b: In the exact center of the lane at all times
choice_c: In the tire tracks left by vehicles, often the left tire track depending on conditions
choice_d: It makes no difference where you ride once it starts raining
explanation: The center of a lane can be hazardous when wet. When it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles -- often the left tire track will be the best position, depending on traffic and roadway conditions.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Where do patches of ice tend to develop first?
choice_a: Ice patches are equally likely everywhere on a roadway
choice_d: In low or shaded areas, and on bridges and overpasses
explanation: Rain dries and snow melts faster on some sections of a road than others. Patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: If a rider absolutely cannot avoid riding on ice or snow, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Keep the motorcycle straight up, proceed as slowly as possible, and stay off the brakes
choice_b: Lean the motorcycle into the turn as usual and brake normally
choice_c: Accelerate quickly to get through the hazard faster
choice_d: Apply the front brake firmly to maintain control
explanation: Cautious riders avoid roads covered with ice or snow. If you can't, keep your motorcycle straight up and proceed as slowly as possible, staying off the brakes; if needed, squeeze the clutch lever and coast.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: When crossing railroad tracks that run roughly parallel to your lane, at what minimum angle should you cross to reduce the risk of the wheel getting caught?
choice_d: Angle doesn't matter for parallel tracks
explanation: For tracks and road seams that run parallel to your path, move far enough away to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn so you're not thrown off balance.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.28, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: When crossing railroad tracks that cross your lane at close to a right angle, what should a rider generally do?
choice_a: Stop completely on the tracks to check for oncoming trains
choice_b: Always turn to cross the tracks at exactly 90 degrees, no matter the lane position
choice_c: Usually it is safer to ride straight within your lane rather than angling sharply, which could put you into another lane
choice_d: Accelerate hard the moment the front wheel touches the tracks
explanation: Usually it is safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks; turning to take tracks at a 90-degree angle can be more dangerous, since the direction may put you into another lane of traffic.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27-28, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: What should a rider do when crossing rain grooves or bridge gratings that cause the motorcycle to weave?
choice_a: Accelerate sharply to power through the weave
choice_b: Zigzag to stay centered in the lane
choice_c: Brake hard immediately to stop the weave
choice_d: Relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across
explanation: Riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings may cause a motorcycle to weave; this uneasy, wandering feeling is generally not hazardous. Relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across -- crossing at an angle forces a more hazardous zigzag.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.28, 'Grooves and Gratings'

question: If a rider must ride over a small obstacle in the road, what technique does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Slow down as much as possible, keep the motorcycle straight, rise slightly off the seat, and roll on the throttle slightly just before contact
choice_b: Accelerate hard right before contact to "jump" the obstacle
choice_c: Brake hard at the moment of contact
choice_d: Approach the obstacle at a shallow, glancing angle
explanation: If you must ride over an obstacle, slow down as much as possible before contact, keep the motorcycle straight, rise slightly off the seat with weight on the footrests, and just before contact roll on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end, then roll off.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: After riding over an object in the street, what should a rider do?
choice_a: Continue riding normally with no further action needed
choice_b: Pull off the road and check the tires and rims for damage before continuing
choice_c: Immediately accelerate to highway speed to test the tires
choice_d: Report it only if a passenger was aboard at the time
explanation: If you ride over an object on the street, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: Where does dirt and gravel tend to collect along a roadway, requiring extra caution?
choice_a: Dirt and gravel are evenly distributed and pose no extra risk anywhere
choice_b: Only in the exact center of the travel lane
choice_c: Along the sides of the road, especially on curves and ramps leading to and from highways
choice_d: Only on gravel roads, never on paved highways
explanation: Dirt and gravel collect along the sides of the road, especially on curves and ramps leading to and from highways. Be aware of what's on the edge of the road, particularly when making sharp turns and getting on or off freeways at high speeds.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Why should a rider watch for oil spots when putting a foot down to stop?
choice_a: It has no bearing on rider safety
choice_b: Oil spots only affect the motorcycle's tires, never a rider's footing
choice_c: Oil spots are only a concern for four-wheeled vehicles
choice_d: The rider may slip and fall on the oil
explanation: Watch for oil spots when you put your foot down to stop -- you may slip and fall.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'
